## Question and method

I used user-to-user collaborative filtering to predict movie ratings from participants with similar rating patterns. Pearson correlation measures similarity. I tested the system by hiding one rating at a time and predicting it from the other 35 ratings.

I also recalculated the Week 3 Global Baseline Estimate for every same training split. This gives both methods the same 36 test cases and prevents the held-out value from entering either calculation.

## Load and verify the data

```{r}
#| label: load-and-check

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

ratings <- read_csv(
  "movie_ratings_query.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

required_columns <- c("participant_id", "movie_title", "rating")

stopifnot(
  identical(names(ratings), required_columns),
  nrow(ratings) == 36,
  n_distinct(ratings$participant_id) == 6,
  n_distinct(ratings$movie_title) == 6,
  !anyNA(ratings),
  all(ratings$rating %in% 1:5),
  !anyDuplicated(ratings[c("participant_id", "movie_title")])
)

data_check <- ratings |>
  summarise(
    participants = n_distinct(participant_id),
    movies = n_distinct(movie_title),
    ratings = n(),
    missing_values = sum(is.na(rating)),
    minimum_rating = min(rating),
    maximum_rating = max(rating)
  )

kable(data_check)
```

The file has `r data_check$ratings` ratings from `r data_check$participants` participants for `r data_check$movies` movies. There are no missing values or duplicate participant-movie pairs.

## Personalized prediction function

The function first calculates the target participant's mean from the training data. It then compares the target participant with each other participant who rated the held-out movie. Similarity is based only on movies that both participants rated in the training data.

```{r}
#| label: personalized-function

predict_personalized <- function(train, target_user, target_movie) {
  target_ratings <- train |>
    filter(participant_id == target_user)

  target_mean <- mean(target_ratings$rating)

  candidate_ratings <- train |>
    filter(
      movie_title == target_movie,
      participant_id != target_user
    )

  similarities <- map_dfr(
    candidate_ratings$participant_id,
    function(other_user) {
      other_ratings <- train |>
        filter(participant_id == other_user)

      shared <- inner_join(
        target_ratings,
        other_ratings,
        by = "movie_title",
        suffix = c("_target", "_neighbor")
      )

      similarity <- NA_real_

      if (
        nrow(shared) >= 3 &&
        sd(shared$rating_target) > 0 &&
        sd(shared$rating_neighbor) > 0
      ) {
        similarity <- cor(
          shared$rating_target,
          shared$rating_neighbor,
          method = "pearson"
        )
      }

      tibble(
        participant_id = other_user,
        similarity = similarity,
        neighbor_mean = mean(other_ratings$rating)
      )
    }
  )

  usable_neighbors <- candidate_ratings |>
    inner_join(similarities, by = "participant_id") |>
    filter(!is.na(similarity), similarity > 0)

  if (nrow(usable_neighbors) > 0) {
    estimate <- target_mean +
      sum(
        usable_neighbors$similarity *
          (usable_neighbors$rating - usable_neighbors$neighbor_mean)
      ) / sum(usable_neighbors$similarity)

    method <- "Pearson collaborative filtering"
  } else {
    estimate <- target_mean
    method <- "User mean fallback"
  }

  tibble(
    personalized_prediction = pmin(5, pmax(1, estimate)),
    prediction_method = method,
    neighbors_used = nrow(usable_neighbors)
  )
}
```

## Fair Week 3 baseline function

The earlier baseline used the global mean plus participant bias plus movie bias. I use the same formula here, recalculated from each 35-row training set.

```{r}
#| label: baseline-function

predict_global_baseline <- function(train, target_user, target_movie) {
  global_mean <- mean(train$rating)

  user_mean <- train |>
    filter(participant_id == target_user) |>
    summarise(value = mean(rating)) |>
    pull(value)

  movie_mean <- train |>
    filter(movie_title == target_movie) |>
    summarise(value = mean(rating)) |>
    pull(value)

  estimate <- global_mean +
    (user_mean - global_mean) +
    (movie_mean - global_mean)

  pmin(5, pmax(1, estimate))
}
```

## Leave-one-out evaluation

Each loop removes exactly one row. Both models receive the same remaining rows and predict the same held-out rating.

```{r}
#| label: leave-one-out

predictions <- map_dfr(
  seq_len(nrow(ratings)),
  function(i) {
    held_out <- ratings[i, ]
    training <- ratings[-i, ]

    personalized <- predict_personalized(
      training,
      held_out$participant_id,
      held_out$movie_title
    )

    baseline <- predict_global_baseline(
      training,
      held_out$participant_id,
      held_out$movie_title
    )

    bind_cols(held_out, personalized) |>
      mutate(
        baseline_prediction = baseline,
        personalized_error = rating - personalized_prediction,
        personalized_absolute_error = abs(personalized_error),
        personalized_squared_error = personalized_error^2,
        baseline_error = rating - baseline_prediction,
        baseline_absolute_error = abs(baseline_error),
        baseline_squared_error = baseline_error^2
      )
  }
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(predictions) == 36,
  all(between(predictions$personalized_prediction, 1, 5)),
  all(between(predictions$baseline_prediction, 1, 5)),
  !anyNA(predictions)
)

write_csv(
  predictions,
  "results/leave_one_out_predictions.csv"
)

kable(
  predictions |>
    select(
      participant_id,
      movie_title,
      rating,
      personalized_prediction,
      baseline_prediction,
      prediction_method,
      neighbors_used
    ),
  digits = 3
)
```

## Accuracy results

```{r}
#| label: accuracy-results

n_cases <- nrow(predictions)

model_metrics <- tibble(
  model = c(
    "Personalized recommender",
    "Week 3 global baseline"
  ),
  MAE = c(
    mean(predictions$personalized_absolute_error),
    mean(predictions$baseline_absolute_error)
  ),
  RMSE = c(
    sqrt(mean(predictions$personalized_squared_error)),
    sqrt(mean(predictions$baseline_squared_error))
  ),
  predictions = n_cases
)

method_counts <- predictions |>
  count(prediction_method, name = "predictions")

write_csv(model_metrics, "results/model_metrics.csv")
write_csv(method_counts, "results/prediction_method_counts.csv")

kable(model_metrics, digits = 3)
kable(method_counts)
```

The personalized system had an MAE of `r sprintf("%.3f", model_metrics$MAE[1])` and an RMSE of `r sprintf("%.3f", model_metrics$RMSE[1])`. The same-split Global Baseline Estimate had an MAE of `r sprintf("%.3f", model_metrics$MAE[2])` and an RMSE of `r sprintf("%.3f", model_metrics$RMSE[2])`.

The Pearson calculation was available for `r sum(predictions$prediction_method == "Pearson collaborative filtering")` predictions. The user-mean fallback was used for `r sum(predictions$prediction_method == "User mean fallback")` predictions. The model with the lower MAE was `r model_metrics$model[which.min(model_metrics$MAE)]`.

```{r}
#| label: metric-plot
#| fig-cap: "Lower MAE and RMSE indicate predictions closer to the actual ratings. Values are printed above each bar."

metric_plot_data <- model_metrics |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(MAE, RMSE),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "error"
  )

metric_plot <- ggplot(
  metric_plot_data,
  aes(x = metric, y = error, fill = model)
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    width = 0.65,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", error)),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    vjust = -0.35,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, max(metric_plot_data$error) * 1.18)) +
  labs(
    title = "Leave-One-Out Error on the Same 36 Ratings",
    x = "Error metric",
    y = "Rating points",
    fill = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggsave(
  "results/model_error_comparison.png",
  metric_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)

metric_plot
```

## Actual and predicted ratings

```{r}
#| label: actual-predicted-plot
#| fig-cap: "The dashed line represents a perfect prediction. Shape and color both identify the model."

actual_plot_data <- predictions |>
  select(
    actual_rating = rating,
    `Personalized recommender` = personalized_prediction,
    `Week 3 global baseline` = baseline_prediction
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -actual_rating,
    names_to = "model",
    values_to = "predicted_rating"
  )

actual_plot <- ggplot(
  actual_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = actual_rating,
    y = predicted_rating,
    color = model,
    shape = model
  )
) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0.08, alpha = 0.72, size = 2.7) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(1, 5), ylim = c(1, 5)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual and Predicted Movie Ratings",
    x = "Actual rating",
    y = "Predicted rating",
    color = "Model",
    shape = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggsave(
  "results/actual_vs_predicted.png",
  actual_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)

actual_plot
```

## Simulated top-three output

Because every person already rated every movie, these rankings show the three highest leave-one-out predictions for each participant. They demonstrate the requested recommendation output, but they are not new viewing suggestions.

```{r}
#| label: simulated-recommendations

recommendations <- predictions |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  arrange(
    desc(personalized_prediction),
    movie_title,
    .by_group = TRUE
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    participant_id,
    rank,
    movie_title,
    personalized_prediction,
    prediction_method
  )

write_csv(
  recommendations,
  "results/simulated_top3_recommendations.csv"
)

kable(recommendations, digits = 3)
```

## Conclusion

The comparison shows whether this small personalized model improves on the earlier baseline. The evaluation covers every rating, uses the same held-out cases, and reports fallback use instead of treating every prediction as Pearson-based.

The main limitation is the size and structure of the survey. There are only six participants, and everyone rated the same six movies. These are simulated predictions of known ratings, not recommendations for movies the participants have not seen. More participants, more movies, and a naturally sparse ratings table would provide a stronger test.
